chapter_title: Introduction to React Navigation: Stack Navigator

screens.title: Introduction to React Navigation — Stack Navigator
screens.subtitle: Why navigation matters and how the stack pattern models native mobile flows

narration.text: In modern mobile apps users expect smooth transitions between views. Navigation is the system that lets an app move from a list to a detail, a dashboard to settings, or a feed to an article. In React Native, React Navigation is the most common library to provide these patterns across platforms. In this lesson we’ll learn why navigation is essential, how a stack navigator models a history of screens, and what you need to install to get started. You will see a compact set of topics — setup, stack wiring, and parameter passing — that combine to make screen-to-screen flows reliable and testable. For example, a product list pushes a product detail screen on top of the stack, and going back pops it off, preserving the user’s previous state. We will also look at common pitfalls like trying to read route parameters when they might be undefined. By the end of the chapter you will be able to install React Navigation, add a NavigationContainer and Stack. Navigator, push and pop screens, and pass data between them safely. Think of navigation as the app’s routing backbone: small mistakes here affect many screens. Ready to explore the key topics and see a concrete two-screen implementation?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: A Stack Navigator models a history of screens: push to add, pop to return, and parameters let screens exchange data safely.

screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives guide practical steps and conceptual understanding. First, you will explain why navigation is necessary in multi-screen mobile apps: users expect back stacks, contextual headers, and preserved state as they move through views. Second, you will be able to install and configure React Navigation and its platform helpers so your app uses native memory optimizations and safe-area handling. Third, you will implement a Stack. Navigator and define Stack. Screen entries to create a push/pop history that feels native. Fourth, you will pass and retrieve parameters between screens safely and use navigation methods like navigate, push, and goBack to control flow. Each objective ties a concept to a developer action — for example, installing react-native-screens improves performance because off-screen views stop rendering, and using navigation. push allows multiple detail pages to stack independently. You’ll practice defensive parameter access to avoid runtime errors when route. params is absent. Together these skills let you build reliable two-screen flows and extend them into multi-screen apps with consistent behavior.

screens.title: Why navigation is necessary
screens.subtitle: From single-screen apps to multi-view user journeys

narration.text: Navigation is the mechanism that connects distinct views in a mobile app, turning isolated screens into an experience that users can move through naturally. When you open a product list and tap an item, you expect the app to show details and let you return without losing context. That expectation is the practical need for navigation: it preserves history, supports back behavior, and enables contextual headers and deep links. In React Native, navigation is more than linking views — it’s about lifecycle, performance, and consistent UX across platforms. A common example is an e-commerce flow: a product list pushes a details screen that displays an item object passed as parameters, and when you go back, the list retains scroll position. A common misconception is treating navigation as merely triggering a render of a new component; instead, it manages a history stack with state and transitions. Practically, design navigation early so component state and data fetching align with screen transitions. Think through whether a view should be pushed on top of an existing instance or should reuse an existing route; that decision affects which method you use later. For reflection: how will your app preserve state when a user navigates away and returns?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Navigation coordinates views, state, and history so users can move between screens predictably.

content.html:
Core Concept

Why navigation is necessary

Navigation turns screens into a journey. Users expect history, back buttons, and preserved state as they move through your app.

Concrete example
Tap a product in a list, view details, then go back to the list with the same scroll position and filters intact.
Common misconception
Navigation is not just rendering a different component. It manages history, transitions, and lifecycle for each screen.
Why it matters
Good navigation preserves user context and prevents surprising state loss when screens are pushed or popped.
Key Takeaway

Treat navigation as app state and lifecycle management, not just view switching.

Definition & Analogy
Stack metaphor
Think of screens as plates stacked. Pushing adds a plate on top; popping removes the top plate to reveal the previous state.
Scenario
User taps three articles in a feed. Each opens its own detail screen so the back button retraces the reading order naturally.

screens.title: Install and configure React Navigation
screens.subtitle: Packages to install and why each one matters

narration.text: Installing React Navigation requires a small set of core and platform-specific packages. First, install the core package @react-navigation/native which provides the navigation container and core logic. Next, add platform helpers such as react-native-screens and react-native-safe-area-context. react-native-screens avoids rendering unfocused screens to save memory and improve performance, while react-native-safe-area-context handles notches and status bars correctly so headers and content do not overlap hardware elements. If you are using Expo, run the Expo installer commands that ensure compatibility. For bare React Native projects run npm install for the native packages and then cd ios && pod install to link iOS dependencies. A frequent developer mistake is skipping pod install on iOS, which leads to runtime errors because native modules are not linked; another is not wrapping the app in NavigationContainer, which prevents any navigator from functioning. Practice by running the install commands and then verifying that NavigationContainer accepts your stack. This step is foundational: without these packages and proper linking there will be subtle crashes or layout issues when navigating. Install and configure React Navigation means install @react-navigation/native, react-native-screens, react-native-safe-area-context; run pod install for ios or use expo installers.. In practical terms, packages to install and why each one matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: NavigationContainer and stack wiring
screens.subtitle: Root container and how Stack.Navigator fits into the tree

narration.text: NavigationContainer is the root provider for all navigators in React Navigation. It maintains navigation state, handles linking, and provides context to child navigators. You must wrap your app with NavigationContainer before adding any navigators like Stack. Navigator. Inside this container, createStackNavigator returns a Stack object with Navigator and Screen components. Stack. Navigator defines the navigation flow and common options, while Stack. Screen registers individual screens with a name and component. For example, adding Stack. Screen name="Home" component={HomeScreen} gives the runtime an entry point, and initialRouteName controls which screen appears first. A common pitfall is placing NavigationContainer below other providers that expect navigation context; keep it at the top-level of navigation logic to avoid undefined navigation objects. You can dynamically set titles via options or setOptions from a screen using the navigation object. When you wire the stack correctly you get predictable header behavior, back gestures, and consistent state across screen transitions. Consider how nested navigators will inherit or override options when designing larger apps. NavigationContainer and stack wiring means wrap navigators in navigationcontainer, then define a stack.navigator with stack.screen entries to register routes.. In practical terms, root container and how stack.navigator fits into the tree. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Wiring pattern
keyIdea.text: Wrap navigators in NavigationContainer, then define a Stack.Navigator with Stack.Screen entries to register routes.

content.html:
Definition

NavigationContainer and stack wiring

NavigationContainer holds the navigation state and must wrap your navigators. createStackNavigator provides the Stack object used to declare screens.

import { NavigationContainer } from '@react-navigation/native';
import { createStackNavigator } from '@react-navigation/stack';

const Stack = createStackNavigator();

function App(){
  return (
    <NavigationContainer>
      <Stack.Navigator initialRouteName="Home">
        <Stack.Screen name="Home" component={HomeScreen} />
        <Stack.Screen name="Details" component={DetailsScreen} />
      </Stack.Navigator>
    </NavigationContainer>
  );
}
How it behaves
  • initialRouteName selects which screen shows first.
  • Stack.Screen name must be unique within a navigator.
  • options and setOptions allow per-screen header customization.
Practical tip
Keep NavigationContainer near your root component so all navigators can access the navigation state without undefined contexts.
Key Takeaway

NavigationContainer is essential—place it at the root, then register Stack.Screen entries inside a Stack.Navigator.

When you copy this pattern into your project, ensure HomeScreen and DetailsScreen are exported components and that native dependencies are installed. A typical mistake is naming the Stack. Screen a different string than the one you navigate to; names must match exactly for navigation methods to resolve. Another tip: use options as a function when you need dynamic titles based on route. params. Run the app and press a button that navigates to Details; if you see the header title and can go back, the wiring is correct. In practical terms, a concrete app.js with navigationcontainer and stack.navigator. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: App.js pattern
keyIdea.text: Use NavigationContainer, createStackNavigator, and Stack.Screen entries with matching names to enable navigation methods.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

Starter App.js

import * as React from 'react';
import { NavigationContainer } from '@react-navigation/native';
import { createStackNavigator } from '@react-navigation/stack';
import HomeScreen from './HomeScreen';
import DetailsScreen from './DetailsScreen';

const Stack = createStackNavigator();

function App() {
  return (
    <NavigationContainer>
      <Stack.Navigator initialRouteName="Home">
        <Stack.Screen name="Home" component={HomeScreen} options={{ title: 'Overview' }} />
        <Stack.Screen name="Details" component={DetailsScreen} />
      </Stack.Navigator>
    </NavigationContainer>
  );
}
export default App;
Ensure the names you use in Stack.Screen match the names you pass to navigation.navigate or navigation.push. If they differ the navigator cannot find the route.
What to check after running
  • The header appears with the title set in options.
  • The back button shows after navigating to Details.
  • No console errors about missing native modules after install.
Misconception
NavigationContainer is not optional. Without it, your Stack.Navigator has no context and screen navigation will fail.
Key Takeaway

Match route names and verify the header/back behavior to confirm wiring is correct.

screens.title: Navigate, push, and goBack — behavior and differences
screens.subtitle: Which method to choose and when

narration.text: React Navigation provides several methods to control the stack. navigation. navigate('Route') finds or creates a route and navigates to it; if that route already exists deeper in the stack, navigate may go back to the existing instance instead of creating a new one. navigation. push('Route') always pushes a new instance of the named screen, which is useful when you want multiple detail screens for different items. navigation. goBack() pops the current screen and returns to the previous one. A concrete use case: in a news app you want each tapped article to open its own detail screen so the user can open several articles and then back through them; that calls for navigation. push. A common confusion is using navigate when you expect multiple instances; navigate may reuse an existing route. Another detail: navigation. setOptions updates header options dynamically from within a screen if you need to change a title based on data. Practically, decide whether you want one unique route instance (navigate) or multiple instances (push) before implementing the behavior, and always test the back stack to ensure it matches user expectations.

keyIdea.title: Action differences
keyIdea.text: Use navigate for route lookup or reuse, push for always-new instances, and goBack to pop the top screen.

content.html:
Comparison

navigate vs push vs goBack

navigation.navigate('Route')
Navigate to a route; may reuse an existing instance deeper in the stack.
navigation.push('Route')
Always push a new instance of a screen, enabling multiple detail pages in history.
navigation.goBack()
Pop the current screen and return to the previous one.
Example scenario
News feed: tapping three different articles should open each in its own detail screen. Use navigation.push so each tap pushes a new instance. If you used navigate and an ArticleDetail route already existed near the top, navigate might return to it instead of creating a new one, which loses the separate reading history.
Misconception to avoid
Assuming navigate always creates a new instance. It may instead move to an existing route with the same name.
Key Takeaway

Choose push when you need distinct instances; use navigate for route reuse and goBack to return.

screens.title: Passing parameters between screens
screens.subtitle: How to send data during navigation and why it's useful

narration.text: Passing parameters during navigation lets you send contextual data to the next screen so it can render relevant content. You can pass parameters by providing a second argument to navigation. navigate or navigation. push, for example navigation. navigate('Details', { itemId: 86, name: 'T-Shirt' }). The receiving screen gets a route prop where parameters live in route. params. Use destructuring with a defensive fallback, for example const { itemId } = route. params || {} to avoid errors if params are missing. Passing objects lets you avoid global state for simple flows: pass a small product object from Home to Details rather than re-fetching it. Be mindful of large objects or functions — prefer IDs for navigation and fetch or cache heavier data in the target screen. A common mistake is destructuring route. params directly when it may be undefined, producing a runtime crash. Test navigation both with and without params to ensure your screen handles missing values gracefully. Finally, dynamic header titles are often built from params using options or options as a function that reads route. params to set the title.

keyIdea.title: Parameter pattern
keyIdea.text: Pass small data objects or IDs as a second argument to navigate/push and access them via route.params with defensive checks.

content.html:
Definition

Passing parameters

// Sending
navigation.navigate('Details', { itemId: 86, name: 'T-Shirt' });

// Receiving
function DetailsScreen({ route, navigation }) {
  const { itemId, name } = route.params || {};
  // defensive access prevents crashes when params are missing
}
Prefer passing IDs for large data and fetch on the Details screen when needed. Small plain objects are fine for quick flows.
Practical notes
  • Always check route.params exists before destructuring.
  • Use optional chaining like route.params?.itemId for concise safety.
  • Set header titles with options={({ route }) => ({ title: route.params?.name || 'Details' })}.
Common mistake
Destructuring route.params without a fallback causes runtime errors when the screen is opened without parameters.
Key Takeaway

Pass small data or IDs and always read route.params defensively to prevent crashes.

screens.title: HomeScreen and DetailsScreen starter code
screens.subtitle: Implement navigation.navigate with params and defensive retrieval

narration.text: We'll examine starter code for HomeScreen and DetailsScreen that demonstrates passing and receiving parameters. HomeScreen creates a productData object and calls navigation. navigate('Details', productData) when the user presses a button. DetailsScreen receives route and navigation props; it destructures route. params using const { id, name, price, description } = route. params || {} so the component handles missing params gracefully. The Details screen then renders fields conditionally and uses navigation. goBack to return. This pattern is simple and effective for many apps. Important details: ensure you export and import these screens correctly and that you pass the same route name used in Stack. Screen. Also, avoid passing functions or deeply nested objects as params; pass identifiers if you need to fetch or load larger data in the target screen. Practice: run the starter code, tap the button to navigate, and inspect the displayed product values as confirmation that parameters flowed correctly. HomeScreen and DetailsScreen starter code means homescreen navigates with an object param; detailsscreen reads route.params with a fallback and conditionally renders values.. In practical terms, implement navigation.navigate with params and defensive retrieval. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Starter pattern
keyIdea.text: HomeScreen navigates with an object param; DetailsScreen reads route.params with a fallback and conditionally renders values.

content.html:
HomeScreen (sender)
// HomeScreen.js
function HomeScreen({ navigation }) {
  const productData = {
    id: 'p101',
    name: 'React Native T-Shirt',
    price: 29.99,
    description: 'A comfortable t-shirt for React Native enthusiasts!',
  };

  return (
    // onPress sends the product object as params
    // navigation.navigate('Details', productData)
    null
  );
}
Replace the null return with your UI and call navigation.navigate when a user taps a product item.
DetailsScreen (receiver)
// DetailsScreen.js
function DetailsScreen({ route, navigation }) {
  const { id, name, price, description } = route.params || {}; // defensive access

  return (
    // Render details if id exists, otherwise show a fallback
    null
  );
}
Key: use route.params || {} to avoid runtime errors when params are missing. Display a friendly message when no data is found.
Pro tip
Prefer sending a small object or an ID. Fetching large data in the target screen keeps navigation lightweight.

screens.title: Header customization and dynamic titles
screens.subtitle: Set static and dynamic header options safely

narration.text: React Navigation provides flexible header customization through the options prop on Stack. Screen and navigation. setOptions inside a screen. You can set a static title using options={{ title: 'Overview' }} on the Stack. Screen node. For dynamic titles that depend on route parameters, use options as a function: options={({ route }) => ({ title: route. params?. name || 'Details' })}. Alternatively, inside a screen component you can call navigation. setOptions({ title: 'New Title' }) when data loads. A common mistake is attempting to access route. params synchronously before data arrives; guard against undefined by providing a fallback. Header styling can be set with headerStyle and headerTintColor inside options to match your brand. Remember that nested navigators may inherit header behavior from parents unless you override it. In practice, prefer options as a function when titles depend on params, and use setOptions for updates after asynchronous fetches so the header reflects loaded content. Header customization and dynamic titles means use static options for fixed titles, options as a function for param-based titles, and setoptions inside screens for dynamic updates.. In practical terms, set static and dynamic header options safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Header patterns
keyIdea.text: Use static options for fixed titles, options as a function for param-based titles, and setOptions inside screens for dynamic updates.

content.html:
Comparison

Static vs Dynamic headers

// Static title
<Stack.Screen name="Home" component={HomeScreen} options={{ title: 'Welcome Home' }} />

// Dynamic title based on params
<Stack.Screen name="Details" component={DetailsScreen} options={({ route }) => ({ title: route.params?.name || 'Details' })} />
Runtime updates
When data loads asynchronously in a screen, call navigation.setOptions({ title: loadedName }) so the header updates. Always guard against undefined params when computing titles to avoid rendering issues.
Practical tip
Use fallback titles until data is available, then update the header to show loaded content for a smoother UX.
Key Takeaway

Choose between static options, options-as-function, or setOptions depending on when and how your title data becomes available.

screens.title: Defensive coding and common pitfalls
screens.subtitle: Avoid runtime errors and unexpected navigation behavior

narration.text: When working with navigation it's common to encounter a few recurring mistakes that break user flows. The most frequent is destructuring route. params without checking for existence; this throws an error when a screen is opened without parameters. Fix this with const { id } = route. params || {} or use optional chaining like route. params?. id. Another pitfall is skipping native linking steps such as pod install on iOS after installing native packages; this produces runtime errors about missing native modules. Also, misnaming Stack. Screen and the name you call from navigation methods leads to failed route resolution. For history behavior, confusion between navigate and push often causes unexpected reuse of existing screens; choose push when you require independent instances. Finally, passing very large objects or functions as params can lead to performance issues or serialization problems; instead pass IDs and fetch larger data on the receiving screen. Testing navigation thoroughly — with and without params, repeated pushes, and back navigation — prevents most issues before they reach users. Defensive coding and common pitfalls means guard route.params, run platform linking, match route names, choose push vs navigate correctly, and avoid large param payloads.. In practical terms, avoid runtime errors and unexpected navigation behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pitfall checklist
keyIdea.text: Guard route.params, run platform linking, match route names, choose push vs navigate correctly, and avoid large param payloads.

content.html:
Common Mistakes

Defensive coding

Undefined params
Always use route.params || {} or optional chaining to avoid crashes when params are missing.
Missing native linking
Run pod install on iOS after adding native modules to avoid runtime errors.
Wrong route names
Ensure the name used in Stack.Screen matches the string you pass to navigate or push.
Performance caution
Avoid passing large objects or functions through navigation parameters. Instead pass an ID and fetch or reference cached data in the target screen to keep navigation payloads small.
Test cases
Open Details with params, open Details without params, open Details multiple times, and verify goBack returns you to the previous state to ensure correct behavior.
Key Takeaway

Defensive patterns and careful testing prevent most navigation-related bugs.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: These three core concepts are the foundation when using a Stack Navigator. First, NavigationContainer is the root context that must wrap your navigators and manages navigation state. Second, the Stack Navigator models push and pop behavior: Stack. Navigator plus Stack. Screen entries define named routes that you navigate between.
